p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for seventeen months, and the countdown clock says 246.
Hana told him she was the one who pushed the 2059 closure, and with his backing she wrote it into the record herself and still leads the root cause.
Garrett merged the stand crew and the high bay into one team under Corinne Mathers, and the ship's three modules are headed to the Cape to launch separately and be joined in orbit.
Before Mars went behind the Sun, he told Ada where things really stand, and that he was scared of the silence.
Then came twenty two days of silence, and when it lifted the first thing through was a medical notice: Ada had been hurt during an oxygen plant repair and discharged a week later.
Corinne Mathers. Leads the new merged Integration and Test team of sixty seven.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Peg Sato. Tallgrass contracts and procurement.
Arlo Dunn. The stand's night technician, thirty one, from Limon.
Wendell Price. Test conductor, now seventy, and the only person who can read the valve by ear.
New in this chapter: Delphine Varga.

Saturday, June 17, 2062. 2:51 AM. He'd sent the request at 12:34 and sat at the kitchen table with the light over the stove on. The round trip was a little over forty two minutes at its fastest. It took two hours and seventeen, because somebody on the station had to find the right form, and somebody else had to ask Ada.

ARES STATION MEDICAL RELEASE TO NEXT OF KIN OKAFOR, ADA. REQUEST RECEIVED SOL 4027. PATIENT CONSENT: YES.. ADMITTED SOL 4013. SCALD, PARTIAL THICKNESS, LEFT FOREARM AND BACK OF LEFT HAND, ABOUT 3 PERCENT BODY SURFACE.. FRACTURES, LEFT RIBS 7 AND 8, NONDISPLACED.. CAUSE: COOLANT RELEASE AND FALL DURING STACK 3 MANIFOLD REMOVAL.. DISCHARGED SOL 4020. LIGHT DUTY 14 SOLS. DRESSINGS DAILY. NO GRAFT REQUIRED AT THIS TIME.. PATIENT ASKS THAT HER FATHER BE TOLD SHE IS FINE AND IS RECORDING.

He read it twice. Then he looked up partial thickness on his phone, which she'd have told him not to do, and learned it meant the second layer of skin and that it hurt more than the deeper kind, because the nerves were still there. He put the phone face down on the table.

It was the last three words of the fifth line he couldn't put down. At this time. He'd learned what those words did in a doctor's mouth in the spring of 2050, in a room at the hospital on Colfax with a window that looked at a parking structure, and he'd hated them for twelve years. He sat with them until the window over the sink went gray.
At 6:05 the Breather team's morning packet came in on the program distribution, where it always came, as if nothing in particular had happened.

ARES STATION BREATHER OPERATIONS ENGINEERING PACKET SOL 4027. No question from Earth today. Sending one answer anyway.. Stack 3 manifold weep worsened Sol 4009. Manifold removed and replaced Sol 4013 to 4016 under station authority (conjunction decision log, line 1). Stack offline 4 sols; stacks 1, 2, 4, 5 carried the load.. One coolant release at removal, 61 C. One injury (Okafor, hydroponics, on loan to the crew). Clamp 2 procedure revised; drain check now signed by two people.. Stack 3 returned to service Sol 4017. Decline rate unchanged from the pre conjunction fit.. Plant log Sol 4005 to 4027 attached for the board's model. C. Okonkwo.
On loan to the crew. He read that line more times than the others.

At 10:40 the mail came, and in it a long white envelope, green ink, Golden postmark. He didn't have to open it to know what day was on the page inside. Everybody who'd been on a flight line in June 2035 knew what day came after the waiver. He held it for a while. Then he put it in the side pocket of his flight bag, the one he'd be carrying to the Cape in four weeks, and zipped the pocket shut. He'd read it there. It seemed like the place it ought to be read.
At 4:52 PM the two note chime. Log twenty five. He was standing at the counter when it came, and he stayed standing.

Ruth's console log. Petrel. Launch Day. L Minus 0. June 12 2035. oh three hundred, on console. chair still wobbles. ticket still open. oh three forty, weather go. range go. wind 8 knots off the water. oh four fifteen, crew at the pad. lise waved at the camera. mori waved at lise. tate humming on the loop. nobody told her to stop. oh six hundred, poll. every station go. prop answered first. wendell. go. he took a second. I heard the second. oh six oh two, FD is go. my voice sounded fine. oh six thirty one, liftoff. oh six forty, orbit. nominal. the room clapped. I let it. oh nine oh five, departure burn prep. isol VLV 2 cycle check. 3 cycles. clean. wrote clean. oh nine twenty one, ignition. burn nominal. oh nine thirty seven, burn nominal. 16 min. oh nine thirty eight, cutoff command. engine down. oh nine thirty eight, isol VLV 2 no close. oh nine thirty eight, tate: VLV 2 shows open. cycling it. oh nine thirty nine, lise: flight, petrel. we have. oh nine thirty nine, loop quiet. oh nine thirty nine, LOS.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4027. One way, 21 minutes 18 seconds. Margin, 437 days. Hi, Dad. Log twenty five. The Sun moved. Medical goes first. It's a rule. I asked them to let this go ahead of it so you'd hear it from me, and they said it's a rule, and I said I know, I wrote half the rules in hydroponics, and they said it's still a rule. So you've read it. I'm sorry you read it at whatever o'clock it was in Aurora. Here's what happened, so you have it from me. Stack three's manifold, the one that was weeping. Okonkwo pulled it in the middle of the quiet, with five of us. Clamp two let go before the loop was all the way drained, and I got a forearm of sixty one degree coolant, and then I got the deck. Two ribs. The arm looks worse than it is. I'm saying that knowing you've already looked up partial thickness. Don't. Okay. You did. Mom's watch is fine. I'd taken it off for the job, because the stack frame eats watches. It was in my chest pocket the whole time. It's still on Aurora time. Twenty two days and I couldn't tell you. That was the worst part. Not the arm. I lay in medical and played your old logs until the nurse asked if I'd like to hear anything else, and then for another week on light duty, until the Sun moved and two of yours came in at once, the ones you recorded in the dark. The one from the twelfth. The woman who told a commander yes. You don't have to tell me who she is. I think I know what kind of yes it was. You sounded like you in both of them. I could hear the refrigerator. The beacon said STATION NOMINAL every sol, including the one where I went into medical. Nominal is the director's word for nobody's dead. I'd like you to know what it covers, in case anybody ever asks you what it means. Okonkwo put the plant log in her packet so the board can rebuild the model. My number off the same log is 437. Stack three held. If it hadn't, you'd be doing harder arithmetic. The other place is fine. Malik kept it alive for a week by himself and he'd like a medal. I told him medals are a fire code violation in a crater. Light duty for fourteen sols, which here means I'm allowed to lift seed trays. 437. Same minus nine. Love you. Log twenty five. Ada out.

He watched it three times. The third time he stopped it where she lifted her left hand to push her hair back, and the dressing ran from her knuckles to her elbow, and she'd tried to keep it out of the frame and hadn't.

Monday, June 26. 7:00 AM. The stage had finished on Stand 2 the Thursday before: its last Watkins hot fire, every cycle of the main oxidizer isolation valve, MOIV-1, under four milliseconds. It was due to fly to the Cape on July 13 on the outsize freighter out of the Colorado Air and Space Port. The integration phase's closeout review was on the calendar for Wednesday.
Garrett's office had sent a note at six. The stage is done. The launch team needs hardware, not a binder. Recommend we skip Wednesday and close the phase after launch.

Corinne Mathers, who ran Integration and Test now, had her legal pad. Forty one open items on the stage, most of them small. Three deviations still unsigned. The physical audit of the propulsion harnesses hadn't been done, because the people who'd do it were the people still on the stand. And she'd promised twenty two of her people to other Tallgrass programs starting July 5. I told them in April, she said. They've told their families.

Quinn put the Cape's receiving checklist beside the pad. It asked, on line nine, for the as built configuration of every propulsion component, by serial number and revision. Nobody at the Cape could fill in line nine. Only the people in this building could.

Wednesday's review runs from seven to four. The physical audit finds one thing that matters: MOIV-1's position sensor harness is revision C on the stage and revision D on the drawing, from a swap during the April work that nobody wrote back into the record. It's verified, the drawing is corrected, and the record says why. The deviations get signed or reopened. The forty one open items become nine that travel, each with a name beside it at the Cape and a name beside it at Watkins. Quinn runs a lessons session for an hour and makes everybody write one thing down. Corinne releases her twenty two on July 5, as promised, and reads their names out in the high bay with one sentence each. At 4:10 Corinne and the Cape's receiving lead sign the handover. Line nine has every cold cycle MOIV-1 ever made in it, counted and signed.

Monday, July 17. He opened page ten in a room on the fourth floor of a hotel in Cocoa Beach, with the air conditioner rattling and the window open anyway, because he wanted to hear the water. He read it once. Then he sat on the end of the bed with it on his knees for a long time, until the light in the parking lot came on.
He'd heard a squadron ops room go quiet once, in Arizona, in 2041. He knew what the bottom of the page sounded like.

Captain Leo Marchetti had called him Chief from the first week, as a joke about how long Sam took over a jet's forms, and then one day he'd stopped joking and kept calling him that. At a family day early that April, two weeks before the surge, he'd found Ada on an upturned helmet bag in the hangar and crouched down and put his cap on her head, the one with the doctor's bag patch. Captain Okafor. That makes you the ranking officer, ma'am. Don't let your dad tell you different. She'd saluted him with the wrong hand. Sam hadn't let himself think about that in years. He thought about it now, with page ten on his knees.

Wednesday, July 19. He watched the board on a feed from a folding table at the Cape. It accepted the margin model the agency had rebuilt from the station's own plant log, without the six spare stacks, and that afternoon the footnote came off. On the agency's own number, for the first time, the ship got there two days after the air ran out. He wrote that on the back of the hotel's room service card and nothing else, and put it in his shirt pocket.
Thursday, July 20. 9:00 AM. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, had one question, in writing, for next Thursday's call: Is the launch campaign in compliance? Yes or no.

Quinn had pulled every requirement the campaign lived under into one spreadsheet. It had 214 lines from four sources: the range, Coquina Launch Services' safety office, the ARA, and the State of Florida. Some were duplicates in different words. Some had owners. Line 61, the propulsion configuration record, was green, signed at Watkins on June 28. Nobody had sorted them into anything.

It takes Quinn and Corinne two days and a whiteboard with four columns: security, health and safety, sustainability, regulatory. The 214 lines become 197. Every one gets an owner, and every owner confirms it in writing. Eleven aren't met yet, and two of those are threats with a date on them: the ARA's thirty day disposal rule for launch 1's upper stage, and the state's transport permit for hot fire 2's methane. For each of the eleven they write what happens if it isn't met, to whom, and when it closes. Sam answers Hale's office the next Thursday at nine. Not yet, ma'am. One ninety seven requirements, all owned. Eleven open, two of them serious, every one with a date. I'll send the list every Friday until it's zero. A pause on the line. Then Hale says, That's a better answer than yes.

Thursday, August 3. Delphine Varga was Coquina Launch Services' mission manager for all three Halcyon launches, which meant she owned the rocket and everything about it that wasn't the payload. She was fifty, ran on iced coffee, and had a whiteboard in her office with the last forty launches from the pad written on it in green and two in red.

The habitat and cargo module had come in 530 kilograms over its contracted mass. Four hundred thirty of that was the six bridge stacks and their mounts, which were on the manifest when it closed on June 1. The rest was the station's medical resupply. Coquina could still lift it. But the heavy lifter's upper stage would reach orbit with very little propellant left, and the ARA's Sustainment Rule S-12 said a spent upper stage had to come down by a controlled burn within thirty days, over empty ocean.

I can do the insertion or I can do the disposal burn, she said. I can't promise you both with a margin I'd sign. I'd like a waiver of S-12 for launch 1. It'll come down on its own, in about fourteen months. Everybody's stages used to.
Line 118 of Quinn's four columns was S-12. It was in the sustainability column, with an owner at the ARA's sustainability office and a red date beside it.
Garrett had already said, by text, that a waiver for one launch was obviously fine. The launch was fifteen days out.

Delphine's trajectory people and the ARA's sustainability office spend a day on the consequences. A stage left to decay on its own wouldn't come down for fourteen months, and for nine of them it would cross, about twice a day, the band of orbits where Halcyon's three modules were going to meet. Then it would come down wherever it came down. The sustainability office says the waiver isn't theirs to give for a collision risk to a crewed assembly, and Delphine says she wouldn't want it if it were. So they find the margin somewhere else. Coquina inserts the module twelve kilometers lower and keeps the disposal burn. The habitat module raises its own orbit with its thrusters, forty kilograms of its own reserve, approved through the change board on Monday with Hana's signature. On August 18 launch 1 flies clean, and the upper stage comes down over the South Pacific ninety seven minutes after separation.

Thursday, August 31. The National Hurricane Center's outlook had an orange X on it east of the Leeward Islands, and a forty percent chance of something in the next seven days. Delphine had pinned it to the wall by the coffee maker. Nobody had said anything about it.

Peg Sato, who handled the program's contracts, had flown down on Tuesday with the Coquina contract in a binder with tabs. She'd read it on the plane twice. She put it on the folding table open at Clause 22.

COQUINA LAUNCH SERVICES LAUNCH SERVICES AGREEMENT TL-61-0402 CLAUSE 22 (EXTRACT). 22.1 Neither party is liable for delay caused by Force Majeure, which includes named tropical storms and hurricanes.. 22.2 The Contractor may stand down launch operations when, in its judgment, weather presents an unacceptable risk to the launch vehicle or personnel.. 22.3 The Contractor will use reasonable efforts to protect the Customer's payload during a stand down.. 22.4 Each party bears its own costs arising from Force Majeure.

It's a nice clause, Peg said. It answers the question nobody asks. Here's what it doesn't say. Who decides to roll back, and whether we get a say. What reasonable efforts means for a stage that needs a nitrogen purge every hour of the day. Whose power runs the purge if theirs goes down. Whether our people can get into the processing facility after a curfew. And who pays for the second rollout if they roll back and the storm misses.
The stage was in Coquina's processing facility, waiting for hot fire 2, due to start Monday. The heavy lifter for launch 2 was due on the pad on Friday for its wet dress rehearsal.

Peg and Delphine meet on Friday at nine with coffee and the contract between them. By six they have a two page letter modification, signed by both companies' contracting officers. The rollback decision is Coquina's, at the trigger in Coquina's own hurricane plan, with Tallgrass told before it's made. The stage's purge during a stand down is Tallgrass's responsibility, with Coquina's facility power, a backup generator connection, and access for Tallgrass's people outside curfew. Costs stay where 22.4 puts them, except a second rollout for a storm that misses, which they split. They add a shared decision log, one page, for the duration of any storm. Peg initials every page and says she's never been happier to read about generators.

Sunday, September 3. The orange X had become a tropical storm at the five o'clock advisory, off the north coast of Cuba, and the hurricane center had given it a name: Hester. By the eleven o'clock advisory that night it was forecast to be a hurricane by Monday evening and to run north along Florida's east coast, offshore, with its closest approach to the Cape on Tuesday night.

The heavy lifter for launch 2 was on the pad. It had finished its wet dress rehearsal on Saturday, fueled and drained, and the plan had been to leave it there until the stage was mated in two weeks. The stage itself was in the processing facility, under a nitrogen purge, waiting for hot fire 2.

Coquina's hurricane plan had a trigger, written in May: roll back to the hangar if the probability of tropical storm force winds at the pad reaches thirty percent, or if the forecast peak gust exceeds the vehicle's rating on the pad. At 11 PM the hurricane center's wind probabilities put the Cape at thirty eight percent. The forecast gust at the pad was seventy five miles an hour. The rating was eighty.
The letter Peg and Delphine had signed on Friday said the rollback was Coquina's call, at that trigger, with Tallgrass told first. Delphine called him at 11:10 to tell him first.

Garrett called at 11:14. Thirty eight percent is a coin toss that's lost a little weight. The rocket's rated for the gust. A rollback is four days by itself, plus whatever the storm costs. Ask her to wait for the morning advisory.

He tells Delphine she has Tallgrass's support, and tells Garrett why in two sentences: the trigger was written for exactly this night, and a rocket rated for eighty doesn't stay on a pad with a forecast of seventy five and an error bar. Coquina calls the rollback at 11:20. Crews start at 4 AM, and by 2 PM Monday the heavy lifter is in the hangar with the doors closed. The stage's storm plan starts at the same time: tanks at positive nitrogen pressure, purge on, the processing facility closed. Tallgrass's thirty eight people at the Cape are released by three with instructions to go inland, to Orlando or farther, and Quinn sends a note to their families saying where everybody is going and when they'll hear next. At 11 PM Monday, Hester is a Category 1 hurricane, and the probability at the pad is sixty one percent.

Monday, September 4. 1:00 PM. The processing facility was an old building, rated for winds of a hundred and ten miles an hour, which was more than Hester was forecast to bring and less than anyone wanted to bet on. Coquina's own ride out team, seven volunteers, would spend the storm in its launch control center six kilometers inland, which was rated for a hundred and fifty.

The stage's purge ran off the facility's nitrogen line. If the facility lost power and the line dropped, humid air would get into the stage's propellant lines in a few hours, and into MOIV-1's seat cavity with them. Hana had said it at the morning call in a flat voice: If that valve gets wet, I can't tell you what anything it does afterward means.
Her proposal was two Tallgrass technicians in the processing facility for the night, to switch the purge to bottles by hand if the line went down.
Arlo Dunn had volunteered before she finished the sentence. He said there'd be two of them, so it was the rule, and that he'd sat out worse weather than this in Limon.
Most of the Cape team was already on the road to Orlando.

He says no to Arlo first, privately, and thanks him, and means both. Then he asks Hana and Wendell what it would take to make the switch without a hand on it. It takes Wendell four hours and twelve nitrogen bottles: a manifold, a regulator with an automatic switchover, and a pressure transducer on the purge line wired to the facility's telemetry uplink, with its own battery. Coquina's ride out team agrees to watch the readout from the control center and call if it moves. Wendell watches it all night anyway from a hotel room in Orlando, on a laptop, in his canvas jacket. At 9:14 PM on Tuesday the facility loses power. At 9:14 and three seconds the switchover goes to bottles. The purge holds until Thursday morning. In the hotel lobby, Arlo from the stand crew reads the line on Wendell's screen and says, Nobody goes out alone. Nobody goes out at all, then. Fine.

Saturday, September 9. Hester had passed forty miles east of the Cape on Tuesday night as a Category 2, and gone on north and out to sea, and left the Space Coast with downed lines, a flooded causeway, and a sky so clear on Friday that it looked like an apology. The curfew lifted Friday at noon. Sam had driven back from Orlando behind a utility truck convoy.

The heavy lifter was fine in its hangar. The processing facility had lost a strip of roof flashing and taken water in a corridor that wasn't the clean room. The stage's purge had held on the bottles from 9:14 Tuesday night until power came back on Thursday, and its pressure trace was a flat line on Wendell's laptop. The propulsion test cell needed its cable trays inspected before anybody chilled anything. The range said it would be back on Monday.

Quinn had the replan on one sheet. Processing had lost eight days, Monday the 4th through Monday the 11th. Hot fire 2 would start Tuesday. Launch 2 had been Thursday, September 21. Now it was Friday, September 29. The plan had carried eleven days of float between launch 2 and the crew launch on January 9, all of it in front of launch 3. The storm had taken eight. Three were left, and the season ran to the end of November.

Hale's public affairs office had announced September 21 on the Countdown to Ares feed in August. Garrett had repeated it to investors. Gwen called at ten. The Director would like to know if September 21 can still be held. She'd rather not walk back a date the week after a hurricane.

Quinn takes the change to the board on Monday morning: launch 2 on September 29, three days of float left, and the reason in one paragraph. With it she shows two recovery options that don't touch a test. A second shift on encapsulation and mate cuts that work from seven days to five, for 1.4 million and twelve more people. Overlapping the pad's post storm sweep with the heavy lifter's rollout prep saves a day, if the range agrees. The risk register gets a new line: a second storm before November 30, with its own trigger. Sam calls Gwen back that Saturday afternoon at four, before any of it goes to the board. No, ma'am. The 29th. Here's what it does to the float, and here's how we'll try to buy some back. I'd say it the same way to the feed. Hale's office posts the 29th on Monday, after the board, with the reason.

Sunday, September 10. 7:00 AM. Garrett had flown in on the first flight into Orlando after the airport opened, and he came into the Tallgrass office at the Cape in a Tallgrass polo and a good mood, which was the thing to watch.

He had a proposal and he'd written it on one page. Delete hot fire 2. Six days. The stage passed its hot fire at Watkins in June, every cycle under four milliseconds. Nothing has happened to it since but a plane ride and a storm it slept through. Mate it Tuesday, launch on the 23rd, and the float goes from three to nine in the worst month of the season. That's not a shortcut. That's arithmetic.
And Aldergrove's bench has run that valve family cold every week since December That's our valve data.

Hana had the verification plan open on her tablet. Hot fire 2 had been added to it in May, after AR 2207 was reopened, and approved by the change board and recorded by the readiness board's clerk: the only cold cycle sequence on the flight valve after shipping, on the ground instrumentation, with Rack A on its own ground bus. The next look after that would be on orbit, on the stage's flight sensors, which sampled at a fifth of the rate. She said it to Garrett directly, and he listened, which was a good sign or a bad one.
Wendell was at the window with his coffee. The bench isn't the valve that's going. That was all.
Hale would be on the phone at eight. Quinn had already put the second shift on the whiteboard as a recovery option: two days for 1.4 million.

Sam asks Garrett for ten minutes alone first, in the hallway, and says it there. Sir, it isn't mine to delete, and it isn't yours. It's in a plan the board approved. If you want it gone, it goes to the board with your numbers and mine side by side, and I'll recommend we keep it. Then he puts the numbers on the whiteboard where everybody can see them: six days and 3.1 million to run it; the chance it finds something, the cost of finding it here, the cost of finding it on orbit. And beside them, a second shift Quinn prices on the spot: two days back for 1.4 million, without touching a test. Garrett reads the board for a long time with his hands in his pockets. You're telling me no. I'm telling you where the week is, sir. Garrett doesn't take it to the board. On the eight o'clock call Hale hears the numbers and says, Keep it. Buy the two days. Hot fire 2 starts Tuesday at six.

Monday, September 11. The launch readiness review for launch 2 was set for Wednesday, September 27, two days before the launch. Quinn had drafted the commit criteria for the stage over the weekend, ten lines, and she'd put DRAFT across the top in red, because she'd learned that from somebody.

HALCYON LAUNCH 2 DEPARTURE STAGE COMMIT CRITERIA (DRAFT 1). 1. Stage structural inspection after storm: complete, no findings open. Owner C. Mathers.. 2. Purge and dew point in propellant lines within limits. Owner H. Iwasaki.. 3. MOIV-1 performance acceptable. Owner TALLGRASS PROGRAM.. 4. Flight software load verified against the configuration record. Owner R. Quintero.. 5. Range flight safety analysis approved. Owner: none listed.. 6. Disposal plan for the upper stage per S-12. Owner D. Varga.. 7. Telemetry encryption keys loaded and verified. Owner: none listed.. 8. Weather at launch within Coquina's rules. Owner D. Varga, C. Mathers.. 9. Open items list reviewed. Status nominal. Owner S. Okafor.. 10. Business decision to fly: go recorded on the poll. Owner G. LYLE.
Hot fire 2 would start in the morning. Nobody had seen a single cold cycle from it yet. That was the point of writing the page today.
Garrett's office had asked, in a note copied to Hale's, that line 10 stay as it was. The CEO signs the go for Tallgrass.

They fix it in an afternoon, with every owner on the call. Line 3 becomes a number: MOIV-1 position disagreement under ten milliseconds on every cold cycle, owner H. Iwasaki, technical authority. Lines 5 and 7 get owners, the range's flight safety lead and Tallgrass's security officer. Line 8 gets one owner, Delphine, with Corinne consulted. Line 9 gets a real threshold: no open item above minor. Line 10 comes off the stage's page, and in its place Quinn writes the escalation rule in her own hand: If a criterion is missed, its owner says so on the poll, and the launch is no go until the readiness board's duty member accepts it in writing. Garrett's office objects to losing line 10. Sam calls Garrett. You sign the business decision to fly, sir, and nobody can take that from you. You can't own the valve line. Neither can I. The page goes out at 6 PM, dated before any data, as DRAFT 2, without the red.
Tuesday, September 12. 7:30 AM. Hot fire 2 had started at six. The 29th, with two days bought back, needed two shifts in the processing facility as soon as the hot fire was done.

Corinne had the roster on her legal pad. Tallgrass had twenty four technicians at the Cape. Nine of them lived in Brevard County and had been hired there. Five of the nine had storm damage at home: two roofs, a flooded ground floor in Titusville, a car under a tree, and a technician named Rosa who'd been sleeping at her sister's with her two kids since Wednesday and had come to work every day anyway.
Garrett's office had sent a note: twelve hour shifts, mandatory, until launch, with a bonus.
Watkins could send eight people from Integration and Test. Six of them had worked launch 1 and held Coquina's facility certification. Two hadn't, and Coquina's certification course took two days.

Corinne talks to every one of the nine by noon, sitting down, one at a time. The five get the week off with pay and the company's storm assistance, and Corinne makes the call to the assistance office herself so nobody has to fill out the form twice. Two of the five say they'd rather work, days only, and they do. Rosa gets a hotel room near the Cape for the three of them, on the program, until her sister's house has power. The six certified people from Watkins fly in Wednesday. The other two take Coquina's course Wednesday and Thursday and are on the roster from Friday, paired with people who've done it before. The second shift starts the night the mating work begins. It holds.

Hot fire 2 had run six days. Every MOIV-1 cycle was under four milliseconds but one, cycle three after the second soak: seven, with a small pressure ripple just after the poppet lifted. Seven was inside the limit that Hana had signed on September 11, before the data. The stage went up on Friday, September 29, at 7:12 in the morning. Sam watched from the roof of the processing facility with the Cape team.

Tuesday, October 3. 9:40 AM. Four days after launch. Flight control at Watkins ran the checkout. Sam was on the loop from the Tallgrass office at the Cape, with Quinn beside him and the window open to the parking lot.
The MOIV-1 checkout was three cold cycles after the stage's first propellant conditioning in orbit. Cycle one, clean. Cycle two, clean. Cycle three.
Flight, prop. MOIV-1, cycle three. Position disagree at close. Four zero milliseconds.

Nobody said anything on the loop for a while. On the screen beside it Quinn put up hot fire 2's cycle three: seven. Beside that, June at Watkins: under four. Aldergrove's cold bench data was one click away.

The checkout procedure said cycles four and five would run in ninety minutes. A man on the Watkins loop, one of the newer flight controllers, said what somebody always says. Run four and five. If they're clean, it's the sensor. Wendell, on the Watkins loop, didn't say anything. Sam could hear him not saying it.

He says it on the loop in one sentence, and the flight director agrees in fewer. The risk register's AR 2207 entry has had a trigger on it since last year: any recurrence in flight checkout. It's fired, so it's an issue now. MOIV-1 is commanded closed and safed, and cycles four and five come off the procedure until somebody decides what they'd be for. Every bit of the checkout data is frozen and copied. Hana opens the issue as I-62-117, linked to AR 2207, owner H. Iwasaki, priority one. By two o'clock the root cause team is on a call: Watkins, the ARA's reviewer, Aldergrove, Building 6, and Rafa's flight software people to rule the sensors in or out with the redundant channel. The board's duty member hears it from Sam at 10:31. The issue log has nine lines by six, each with a name and a date. Wendell, on the Watkins loop, says one word. Copy.
Wednesday, October 4. 6:30 AM. I-62-117 had nine lines in its log and an owner. The board's duty member had been told at 10:31 the morning before.
Simon Greaves's feed had run a twelve second item at midnight: Sources say Halcyon's departure stage checkout has paused. Somebody in flight control had a cousin. It always was somebody's cousin.

Frances Odum had texted at 6:02. Is it the valve. No question mark. Families of Ares had had a long summer. The agency's own margin had dropped below the arrival day in July, and she'd spent August explaining to two hundred families what two days meant.

Hale's public affairs office had a statement ready for nine. Halcyon's departure stage is performing nominally in orbit. Routine checkout continues. Every word of it was true of everything on the stage but one valve.
Commander Yusra Haddad was in Houston. Her crew would sit on that valve for the whole departure burn, and she found out about things from break rooms when nobody called her first.

Sam calls Yusra at 6:45, before anything else. She listens without interrupting and then asks for the data, and he sends it. At nine the board's clerk has a two page report: the event, the data beside June's, the issue owner, what's known, what isn't, and when the board will hear next. At one he's on a call with Frances and the families' committee. Ma'am, the valve that matters most on the ship did something on orbit yesterday morning that it's done before on the ground. We don't know why yet. Nobody's aboard and nobody's in danger today. Here's what we'll know by when, and you'll hear it from me before you hear it anywhere else. At four the program posts the same thing, in the same words. Hale reads it at three thirty and changes one comma. Frances texts at five. You called before the feed did.

Thursday, October 5. 6:40 AM. He took page ten out of the side pocket of his flight bag and walked across A1A in the dark, past the hotel's boardwalk, to the beach. There was a lifeguard stand with a 7 stenciled on it, shut up for the season, and he sat on its bottom step. The tide was going out. It was warm already, and the sky over the water was going from black to gray along a line that didn't seem to be anywhere in particular.

He read the page by the light from his phone. He knew it by now. He read it anyway, slowly, line by line, the way he'd once read a jet's forms before he signed them, looking for the line that would be different this time. 0905 ISOL VLV 2 CYCLE CHECK. 3 CYCLES. CLEAN. WROTE CLEAN.
LOS. Three letters. It didn't mean they'd stopped. It meant nobody on the ground could hear them anymore.

He had a seven to lay beside the forty, and an under four from Watkins in June. Three points on a line nobody understood yet. It wasn't an answer. It was the one thing he'd done that month that he was sure of.

I-62-117 had fourteen lines in its log by now, each with a name and a date. Hana had slept four hours. Nell, at Aldergrove, had sent him a photograph of one of her father's June letters to the board, with cycle three circled, and no words at all.
Frances had sent a photograph of the program's note on her refrigerator, under the magnet shaped like Colorado.
Wendell had sent him the purge trace from the night of the storm, printed and photographed, with a note in pencil on it. Flat as a board. Like I said.
He made a list in the notebook of what had held since June. It was longer than the other one. He read it to the water, which was what he had instead of a kitchen.

Up the coast, past the point, the pads were lit like a town. He'd worked in their shadow all summer and hadn't once looked at them like this. The last time he had was December of 2058, at a fence by the crew bus, in the dark, telling his daughter her mother would never have let her go. He'd told himself for nearly four years that it was true, and that he'd only said it badly. Sitting on the step with the tide going out, he wasn't sure anymore that it was true.
At 7:40 he went back up to the room and sat at the desk by the window and recorded a log to Ada. One way, nineteen minutes and twenty two seconds.

He told her about page ten. Not all of it. A flight director he knew, a ship, a valve that chattered in a test and was closed anyway, and three letters at the bottom of a page. Then he told her that the valve on his ship had done the same thing on orbit this week, and that he'd told everyone who needed to know, in order, and that now he was telling her. He told her how her arm looked in the frame when she pushed her hair back. He said he'd seen it. He didn't do the voice.
At 11:48 PM his phone lit up on the nightstand. Simon Greaves.
Mr. Okafor. I've been sent the closure record for AR 2207, dated September 19, 2059, with a cover note. I'm on air at nine Mountain. I'd rather have your account in it than not. S.G.
He read it sitting up, with the window open and the water going on outside it in the dark. Fifteen hundred miles west, in an empty high bay in Watkins, the countdown said 136.
